frame: Two texts describe the old Crowley homestead. One is a museum plaque; the other is a ghost tour flyer.
text: MUSEUM PLAQUE: The Crowley homestead was built from local sandstone in 1884 by Elsie and Tom Crowley, who ran sheep on the surrounding land for thirty years. The house has six rooms, a cellar and a stone water tank that still holds rain. After the family moved to the coast in 1914, the homestead stood empty until the island council restored it in 1998. Elsie kept a diary for every year she lived there, and eleven of those diaries are now displayed in the front room. Visitors can also see the original iron stove, the shearers' bunks and a rocking chair Tom made from a fallen river red gum. The homestead is open from 10 am to 4 pm on weekends. frame: Indi is writing an entry for the island's online encyclopedia. Encyclopedia entries must be objective.
text: THE BLUSTER ROCK BUSH BAND is a folk band formed in 1979 by four sheep shearers who played together in the woolshed after work. The original members were Gwen Pike on fiddle, Reg Pike on accordion, Hamish Doyle on guitar and Lou Tran on the tea-chest bass, a home-made instrument built from a wooden box, a broom handle and a single string. Over forty years, the band has released nine albums and played at more than 2,000 dances, weddings and country shows. In 2006, Reg Pike died suddenly, a week before the band's biggest concert, and his grandson Archie took over the accordion at seventeen. Archie still plays his grandfather's accordion, which has a patch of tape over one of its keys. The band's most requested song is 'Dust on the Woolshed Floor', written by Gwen Pike in 1981 about a shearing competition. In 2019, the island council gave the band an award for forty years of music. Critics have described the band's sound in very different ways. One reviewer called it 'joyful and foot-stomping', while another wrote that it was 'old-fashioned and painfully repetitive'. The band still rehearses every Thursday night in the same woolshed, which now has electric lights and a sign on the door asking visitors to wipe their boots.

frame: Mo reviewed the movie 'Wombat Warrior 3' for the crew's newsletter. Tully says it is subjective. Mo wants to know why.
text: WOMBAT WARRIOR 3: A REVIEW BY MO. I watched Wombat Warrior 3 at the Bluster Rock drive-in on Friday night, sitting on the roof of the ute with a bag of lollies. The film runs for three hours and four minutes, which is about two hours longer than it needs to be. It stars a wombat called Digby, who has to stop an evil cockatoo from stealing the island's water supply. The first two films were fun, but this one is tedious, overrated and painfully slow. The jokes are tired, and the big battle scene in the middle is a confusing mess of fur and feathers. The cockatoo gets most of the best lines, while the wombat mostly grunts. The ending sets up a fourth film, which the drive-in owner says will be shown next winter. There is no extra scene after the credits, so you can leave as soon as the music starts. The drive-in charges $12 per car. The only good part is the theme song, which is catchy enough that I hummed it all the way home. Somehow, the film has already made more money than the other two put together. I give it one and a half lollies out of five. Gus loved it, but Gus also likes eating paste.
prompt: Why is Mo's review subjective rather than objective?
answerWith: the text of the one correct option
options: It uses judgement words like 'tedious' and 'overrated', which another viewer could disagree with.
It gives numbers like 'three hours and four minutes', which show the writer's view.
It uses 'I', as in 'I watched it on Friday', which makes any sentence an opinion.
It complains about the film, and only complaints like 'painfully slow' count as opinions.
